Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. Here's a step-by-step guide to boiling an egg: ### Materials Needed: - Eggs - A saucepan or pot - Water - A timer - A slotted spoon or ladle - A bowl of ice water ### Instructions: 1. **Choose Your Eggs:** - Start with eggs that are a few days old. Fresh eggs can be harder to peel when hard-boiled. 2. **Prepare the Pot:** - Place the eggs in a single layer in a saucepan or pot. Do not stack them. 3. **Add Water:** - Fill the pot with cold water until the eggs are covered by about an inch (2.5 cm) of water. 4. **Heat the Water:** - Place the pot on the stove over medium-high heat. 5. **Boil the Eggs:** - Wait for the water to come to a rolling boil. 6. **Adjust the Heat:** - Once the water is boiling, reduce the heat to a simmer (a gentle boil). 7. **Set Your Timer:** - Decide how you want your eggs: - **Soft-Boiled:** Simmer for 4–6 minutes. The yolk will be runny and the white will be just set. - **Medium-Boiled:** Simmer for 7–9 minutes. The yolk will be slightly runny to mostly firm. - **Hard-Boiled:** Simmer for 10–12 minutes. The yolk will be fully set and dry. 8. **Prepare Ice Water:** - While the eggs are cooking, prepare a bowl of ice water to stop the eggs from cooking further. 9. **Stop Cooking:** - When the timer goes off, use a slotted spoon or ladle to transfer the eggs from the pot to the bowl of ice water. Let them sit in the ice bath for at least 5 minutes. This eases peeling and prevents overcooking. 10. **Peel the Eggs (Optional):** - Crack the egg all over by gently tapping it on a hard surface, then roll it between your hands to loosen the shell. Peel the shell off starting at the larger end, which often has an air pocket. 11. **Serve:** - Your eggs are ready to eat as desired. ### Tips: - For easier peeling, you can add a teaspoon of vinegar or a pinch of baking soda to the boiling water. - Store leftover boiled eggs (in their shells) in the refrigerator for up to a week.

You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Step 1: Make the Crust 1. In a large bowl, combine 2 ½ cups all-purpose flour, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1 teaspoon sugar. 
2. Add 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter, chilled and diced, to the flour mixture. 
3. Using a pastry cutter or your fingers, blend until the mixture resembles coarse crumbs.

6. Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes. 
Step 2: Prepare the Filling 
1. Peel and thinly slice enough apples to yield 6 to 8 cups. 
2. In a large bowl, toss the sliced apples with 1 tablespoon lemon juice to prevent browning. 
3. Add ¾ cup granulated sugar, ¼ cup brown sugar, 2 teaspoons ground cinnamon, ¼ teaspoon ground nutmeg, and ¼ teaspoon salt to the apples. 4. Sprinkle 2 tablespoons all-purpose flour over the apple mixture. Mix until the apples are evenly coated. 
Step 3: Assemble the Pie 
1. Preheat your oven to 425°F (220°C). 
2. Roll out one disk of chilled dough on a lightly floured surface. Fit it into a 9-inch pie pan. 
3. Fill the crust with the prepared apple mixture, slightly mounding it in the center. 4. Dot the top of the apple filling with 1 tablespoon unsalted butter, cut into small pieces. 
5. Roll out the second disk of dough and place it over the filling. 
6. Trim the excess dough and crimp the edges to seal the crust. 
7. Cut several small slits in the top crust to allow steam to escape, or create a lattice design. 
8. Optional: Brush the top crust with a beaten egg and sprinkle with additional sugar.

Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

9. **Peel the Eggs:** - Gently tap the eggs on a hard surface to crack the shell, then peel under running water or in the ice bath to help remove the shell easily.

You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

- 6 to 8 tablespoons ice water

- 6 to 8 cups of thinly sliced, peeled apples (Granny Smith, Honeycrisp, or a mix)
- 3/4 cup sugar

- 1 tablespoon lemon juice
- 2 tablespoons unsalted butter

3. **Add Water**: Sprinkle 1 tablespoon of ice water at a time over the mixture, stirring with a fork until the dough begins to come together. Add just enough water until the dough holds together without being wet or sticky.

#### Prepare the Apple Filling:

5. **Preheat Oven**: Preheat your oven to 425°F (220°C).

12. **Initial Bake**: Place the pie on the middle rack of the oven and bake for 15 minutes at 425°F (220°C).

13. **Reduce Heat**: Reduce the temperature to 350°F (175°C) and continue baking for 35 to 45 minutes, or until the apples are tender and the crust is golden brown. If the edges brown too quickly, cover them with strips of aluminum foil.

14. **Cool**: Allow the pie to cool on a wire rack for at least 2 hours before serving. This will help the filling set.

Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

--- ### Apple Pie Recipe #### 
Ingredients 
**For the Pie Crust:** - 2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour - 1 teaspoon salt - 1 teaspoon sugar - 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter, chilled and diced - 6-8 tablespoons ice water 
**For the Apple Filling:** - 6 to 8 apples (such as Granny Smith or Honeycrisp), peeled, cored, and sliced - 3/4 cup sugar - 2 tablespoons all-purpose flour - 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon - 1/4 teaspoon ground nutmeg - 1 tablespoon lemon juice - 2 tablespoons unsalted butter, cut into small pieces 
**For the Top (Optional):** - 1 egg yolk - 1 tablespoon milk --- ### 

Instructions 
#### Make the Pie Crust 
1 .**Mix Dry Ingredients:** Combine the flour, salt, and sugar in a large bowl. 2. **Cut in Butter:** Add diced butter to the flour mixture. Use a pastry cutter or your hands to blend until the mixture resembles coarse crumbs. 
3. **Add Ice Water:** Gradually add ice water, 1 tablespoon at a time, mixing until the dough holds together. Use 6-8 tablespoons as needed. 
4. **Form and Chill Dough:** Divide dough in half, form into disks, wrap in plastic wrap, and chill for at least 1 hour. 
#### Prepare the Filling 
5. **Preheat Oven:** Set oven to 425°F (220°C). 
6. **Mix Filling Ingredients:** In a large bowl, toss apples with sugar, flour, cinnamon, nutmeg, and lemon juice until coated. #### Assemble the Pie 7. **Roll Out Dough:** On a floured surface, roll out one dough disk into a 12-inch circle. Place in a 9-inch pie pan. 
8. **Add Filling:** Fill crust with the apple mixture and dot with butter pieces. 
9. **Top Crust:** Roll out remaining dough and cover the pie, or cut strips for a lattice top. 
10. **Seal and Trim:** Trim excess dough, fold edges under, and crimp to seal. 
11. **Venting or Glazing (Optional):** Make slits in the top for steam to escape, or brush with an egg yolk and milk mixture for a shiny finish. 

#### Bake the Pie 
12. **Bake:** Place pie on a baking sheet. Bake at 425°F for 15 minutes. Reduce to 350°F (175°C) and bake for an additional 35-45 minutes until apples are tender. 
13. **Cool:** Let the pie cool on a wire rack for at least 2 hours to set before serving. 
--- Enjoy making and eating your delicious homemade apple pie!

You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)
