task2.1: Summarize the following article in one sentence: Help! Can an Airline Really Do That to Me? You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. Ingredients
For the Pie Crust
2 ½ cups all-purpose flour

1 teaspoon salt

1 tablespoon granulated sugar

1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter, chilled and diced

6–8 tablespoons ice water

For the Apple Filling
6–8 cups thinly sliced, peeled apples (about 6–8 medium apples, such as Granny Smith, Honeycrisp, or a mix)

¾ cup granulated sugar

2 tablespoons all-purpose flour

1 teaspoon ground cinnamon

¼ teaspoon ground nutmeg

1 tablespoon lemon juice

1 teaspoon vanilla extract

2 tablespoons unsalted butter, cut into small pieces

For the Top Crust
1 egg yolk

1 tablespoon milk

Optional: 1 tablespoon coarse sugar for sprinkling

Instructions
Make the Pie Crust
Mix Dry Ingredients: In a large bowl, combine the flour, salt, and sugar.

Cut in Butter: Add the chilled, diced butter. Use a pastry cutter or your hands to work it in until the mixture looks like coarse crumbs.

Add Water: Slowly drizzle in the ice water, 1 tablespoon at a time, mixing until the dough just comes together. Avoid overworking.

Form Dough Balls: Divide the dough in half, shape into disks, wrap in plastic, and refrigerate for at least 1 hour (or overnight).

Prepare the Apple Filling
Preheat Oven: Preheat to 425°F (220°C).

Mix Filling Ingredients: In a large bowl, toss apples with sugar, flour, cinnamon, nutmeg, lemon juice, and vanilla until evenly coated.

Assemble the Pie
Roll Out Bottom Crust: On a lightly floured surface, roll one dough disk to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Gently press it into the pan.

Fill the Pie: Spoon in the apple filling, mounding slightly in the center. Dot with butter.

Roll Out Top Crust: Roll the second dough disk for the top. Optionally create a lattice or decorative pattern.

Seal and Trim Edges: Place the top crust, trim excess dough to leave a 1-inch overhang, tuck edges under, and crimp to seal.

Add Vents: Cut small slits on top if using a whole crust (skip for lattice).

Finish and Bake
Egg Wash: Beat the egg yolk and milk together. Brush over crust; sprinkle with coarse sugar if desired.

Bake: Set pie on a baking sheet. Bake at 425°F (220°C) for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350°F (175°C) and bake 35–45 more minutes, until golden and bubbly.

Cool: Let the pie cool on a rack for at least 2 hours before serving to allow filling to set.

Enjoy your warm, homemade apple pie!

Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. Here's a step-by-step guide to help you make a classic apple pie. ### Ingredients: #### For the Pie Crust: - 2 ½ cups all-purpose flour - 1 teaspoon salt - 1 teaspoon sugar - 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter, chilled and cubed - 6 to 8 tablespoons ice water #### For the Apple Filling: - 6 to 8 apples (such as Granny Smith, Honeycrisp, or a mix), peeled, cored, and sliced - ¾ cup granulated sugar - ¼ cup packed brown sugar - 2 tablespoons all-purpose flour - 1 tablespoon lemon juice - 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon - ¼ teaspoon ground nutmeg - ¼ teaspoon salt - 1 tablespoon unsalted butter, cut into small pieces (to dot the filling) #### Optional (for the top of the pie): - 1 egg yolk - 1 tablespoon milk - Coarse sugar for sprinkling ### Instructions: #### Make the Pie Crust: 1. **Mix Dry Ingredients**: In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, salt, and sugar. 2. **Cut in Butter**: Add the chilled, cubed butter to the flour mixture. Use a pastry cutter or your fingers to blend until the mixture resembles coarse crumbs with pea-sized bits of butter. 3. **Add Water**: Sprinkle ice water over the mixture a tablespoon at a time, mixing with a fork or your hands until the dough starts to hold together. Add just enough water to make the dough cohesive but not wet. 4. **Form Dough**: Divide the dough into two equal portions. Shape each portion into a disk, wrap in plastic wrap, and chill in the refrigerator for at least an hour. #### Prepare the Filling: 5. **Prep Apples**: In a large bowl, combine the sliced apples with granulated sugar, brown sugar, flour, lemon juice, cinnamon, nutmeg, and salt. Toss until the apples are evenly coated. #### Assemble the Pie: 6. **Preheat Oven**: Preheat your oven to 425°F (220°C). 7. **Roll Out Dough**: On a lightly floured surface, roll out one disk of dough to fit your pie pan with a little overhang. Transfer the dough to the pie pan. 8. **Fill with Apples**: Pour the apple filling into the crust, mounding it slightly in the center. Dot with butter pieces. 9. **Top Crust**: Roll out the second disk of dough. You can place it over the apples as a whole top crust, create a lattice, or use cookie cutters for a decorative top. 10. **Seal Edges**: Trim the edges of the top and bottom crusts, leaving about a ½ inch overhang. Tuck the excess underneath and crimp with a fork or your fingers to seal. 11. **Ventilate and Brush**: If using a whole top crust, cut several slits to allow steam to escape. Whisk the egg yolk with milk and brush it over the crust for a golden finish. Sprinkle with coarse sugar if desired. #### Bake the Pie: 12. **Initial Bake**: Place the pie on a baking sheet (to catch any drips) and bake in the preheated oven for 20 minutes. 13. **Reduce Temperature**: Lower the oven temperature to 375°F (190°C) and continue baking for 35 to 45 minutes, or until the crust is golden and the filling is bubbly. You may need to tent the edges with aluminum foil if they brown too quickly. 14. **Cool**: Let the pie cool on a wire rack for at least 2 hours before serving to allow the filling to set. Enjoy your homemade apple pie with a scoop of vanilla ice cream or a dollop of whipped cream!

The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. task2.1: Summarize the following article in one sentence: Help! Can an Airline Really Do That to Me? You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

task2.1: Summarize the following article in one sentence: Help! Can an Airline Really Do That to Me? You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

task2.1: Summarize the following article in one sentence: Help! Can an Airline Really Do That to Me? You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

You will first need to make the apple pie crust. To do this, you need flour (2.5 cups), salt (1 tsp), sugar (1 tsp), unsalted butter (2 sticks), ice water (0.5 cup). To make the crust:

1. Combine the flour, salt, and sugar. Whisk until well-combined.
2. Use a hand mixer to mix in most of the butter. Use smaller, cut up pieces for easier mixing. Leave a couple small pieces for later.
3. Slowly mix in 1/4 cup of the ice water and mix until crumbly. Dough should hold together when squeezed. Add more water 1 Tbsp at a time if needed. 
4. Split this dough into half. Form each dough into a disk 3/4 inch thick and then wrap each tightly in plastic wrap. 
5. Refrigerate until firm (at least 1 hour). 

To make the pie, you will need Granny Smith apples (3 pounds), lemon juice (1 Tbsp), Sugar (2/3 cup), all-purpose flour (3 Tbsp), Cinnamon (1/2 tsp), allspice (1/4 tsp), nutmeg (1/4 tsp), vanilla extract (1 tsp), the pie crust dough we made earlier, 1 large egg yolk, cream (1 Tbsp).

To make the pie: 

1. Peel, core, and slice the apples to 1/4 inch slices. 
2. Toss the apple slices in the lemon juice.
3. Combine the sugar, flour, and spices. Add this mixture to the apple slices and use your hands to coat everything evenly. 
4. Sprinkle the vanilla on this mixture and toss again.
5. Preheat the oven to 375 degrees Fahrenheit. 
6. Pull out pie crust dough and let sit at room temperature for 10 minutes. 
7. Roll out both doughs to 12-inch circles and place one onto a 9-inch pie plate.
8. Add the apple filling to the pie plate.
9. Place the other dough circle on top of the pie filling. 
10. Trim excess dough, leaving 3/4 inch overhang.
11. Pinch together the two dough disks and use a fork to secure them all the way around.
12. Use a fork to combine the cream and egg yolk in a bowl and brush this all over the exposed dough. 
13. Place pie in oven and bake at 375F for about 20 minutes and then reduce the heat to 350F. Then bake until the center of the pie reaches 200F on a thermometer. 
14. Transfer to a cooling rack for at least 1 hour before serving.

task2.1: Summarize the following article in one sentence: Help! Can an Airline Really Do That to Me? You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit. That is what travel insurance is for. You Might Need a Doctor’s Note. Turkish Airlines once required passengers with Parkinson’s disease to present a fit-to-fly letter from a doctor. Judy of Chapel Hill, N.C., discovered this rule only at the airport, where an in-airport doctor charged around $400 for a last-minute letter. The airline has since removed the requirement and reimbursed the cost. Don’t Take Their Word for It. Verbal promises are worthless. Jean from Berkeley, Calif., was told by a United worker that the airline would compensate her after a canceled flight, but United later refunded only the ticket cost, not the additional expenses. Airlines are not required to book you on another carrier or honor verbal assurances. As I waited in line at an Air France counter after missing a connection in Paris, the agent carefully avoided promising hotel reimbursement because European compensation rules likely did not apply. She got us on the final flight of the day, which is good, because last-minute hotel rooms in Paris do not come cheap. (1047 words)

task2.1: Summarize the following article in one sentence: Help! Can an Airline Really Do That to Me? You may be surprised by the little-known and sometimes nonsensical rules lurking in the fine print. Here are a few that tripped up readers in 2025. Dear Readers, Let’s end 2025 with a hypothetical tale of terrible travel luck. On your way from New York to London and Paris with your partner, someone swipes your bag from the overhead bin. The airline says sorry, but it takes no responsibility for carry-ons. You shrug it off and end up having so much fun in England that you extend your stay, skipping your flight to Paris and catching a train there a few days later. But as you’re getting ready to leave Paris, you notice your return flight to New York no longer appears on the airline app. When you call, the airline says it canceled your flight after you didn’t show up for the middle leg of your itinerary. So you buy new tickets, but in the stress of the situation you transpose your and your partner’s middle names, and when you get to the airport, they won’t let you check in. Now, you have to trade in your tickets for even pricier last-minute ones. Back home, you eventually persuade the airline to give you a credit for the original voided flight, good for a year. Nine months later, you try to book a new trip and find the credit has expired. Then you write to Tripped Up to complain. I write back with bad news: The rules governing air travel may be complex and sometimes nonsensical, but the airline did not break any of them. Here are five of those rules (and one rule of thumb). Disagree with them at will, but ignore them at your own risk. Skip One Leg, Lose the Rest. If a passenger does not show up for one flight, in many cases most airlines instantly void the remainder of their flights to open up inventory for other travelers. And once those flights are gone, readers report, customer service workers say they can’t bring them back — for the same price, at least. It’s a plausibly defensible rule applied in an often draconian way. Take Stephen of Lyme, Conn., who wrote to me after he and his travel partner missed the first leg of their round-trip itinerary on Emirates (from New York to Delhi via Dubai) because they confused a.m. and p.m. They ended up paying more than $3,000 extra to rebook the whole itinerary and stay overnight at a hotel. Emirates did not respond to my requests for comment, but I suspect the airline might claim it was just following the rules. Instead of canceling, couldn’t carriers just email or text no-shows and say, “Hey, we noticed you missed your flight. Click ‘yes’ to preserve the remaining legs, or ‘no’ to cancel the rest of the itinerary”? Until that happens, call the airline as soon as you know you’ll miss the leg and ask to preserve the rest of your trip. Watch Your Stuff. When 92-year-old Virginia of Washington wrote to me in January to say her $180 Ralph Lauren jacket disappeared after an American Airlines flight attendant offered to hang it up, I thought we had an open-and-shut case. But Andrea Koos, a spokeswoman for the airline, passed along its very clear rules on the matter: Like most other airlines, American takes no responsibility for items you carry on the plane. Instead, it’s an issue for the police. In this case, American did reimburse Virginia in March, but that’s what media pressure and a sympathetic victim will get you. If you lose a carry-on item, report it to a member of the crew or to the airport police and hope your travel, homeowner’s or renter’s insurance will cover it. Get Your Name Right. Our names are the first things we learn to write, yet many readers manage to mess them up when they purchase an airline ticket. Make sure your name matches the name on the ID you will use to fly. If you don’t reserve directly with the airline, things get more complicated. Gary of New York City booked flights through American Express for him and his partner to fly from Newark to Athens on Emirates but filled in “Mike” instead of Michael. At the airport, an Emirates representative said she could have made the minor change if he had booked directly, but in this case the travel agency had to do it. American Express could not, and the couple spent an additional $7,000 to rebook. Do yourself a favor and check your name as soon as your reservation email arrives. When a Year Lasts Eight Months. If you have to cancel a nonrefundable ticket, airlines sometimes offer flight credit, typically good for a year. Some airlines start the clock on the date you purchased the ticket. Young Ju of East Syracuse, N.Y., complained that her Air Canada credit expired less than eight months after her flight. Air Canada explained that tickets are contracts with finite end dates set at the time of purchase. Bonus tip: If you get sick before a flight, airlines are not required to offer a refund or credit.
